questions.title: Why does the D.C. Circuit grant deference to the agency on the law enforcement purpose requirement yet review the decision de novo?
questions.question_body: In this opinion, the court states that while it reviews the summary judgment de novo under FOIA, it also grants deference to the FBI regarding its invocation of Exemption 7(A). I am confused about how deference exists in a de novo review. Does deference prevent the court from independently analyzing the evidence, or does it weigh heavily during the de novo assessment? What is the doctrinal line between deferring on the agency's expertise and reviewing the application de novo?

questions.title: Why does the D.C. Circuit accept a 'conclusory' declaration that an investigation remains 'ongoing' despite the passage of significant time since the initial request?
questions.question_body: The plaintiff argued that years have passed since the initial filing and that the FBI's assertion that investigations are 'ongoing' was too vague under the precedents. However, the D.C. Circuit found the declaration sufficient because of the context and prior declarations. Can you explain why 'vague' assertions regarding 'ongoing investigations' do not automatically expire an agency's ability to hide information under Exemption 7(A) months or years later? What factors 'counseled against' looking at the declaration in isolation?

questions.title: What is the specific 'nexus' burden the government must meet to establish records were compiled for law enforcement purposes under Campbell?
questions.question_body: In Section IV.A, the court quotes Campbell v. DOJ regarding the 'nexus between the investigation and one of the agency’s law enforcement duties.' In practice, how specific must the agency's declaration be regarding this nexus to satisfy Exemption 7(A)? Is it enough to state a person had 'connections' to violence, or does the agency need to detail how the investigation specifically fulfills a federal law enforcement duty?

questions.title: Is a FOIA plaintiff required to oppose an agency's use of ex parte declarations, or does that create an automatic basis for respecting the agency's findings?
questions.question_body: Regarding Section V, the court notes that Farahi forfeited his challenge to the district court's reliance on ex parte declarations because he did not oppose the agency's motion to file them under seal. I understand ex parte filings raise concerns under FOIA. Does a plaintiff's failure to object during the lawsuit effectively waive their ability to argue that the ex parte submission itself was the only basis for withholding agreement? Why does the court rely on affidavits given a separation regarding the standard?

questions.title: What statutory standard does the D.C. Circuit apply to distinguish between 'randomly interspersed' and 'inextricably intertwined' documents under the Mead test?
questions.question_body: The court discusses segregability in Section V, citing Mead Data Cent., Inc. and noting that a 'small amount... interspersed line-by-line' is not likely to be reasonably segregable. How does the court determine when information is not 'randomly interspersed' versus when the exempt content creates an 'inextricable' mix? In FOIA cases, why is the 'focus' on information rather than just words, and does that distinguish the lines between releasable and withheld data?

questions.title: Why did the plaintiff forfeit his arguments regarding 'overbroad' categories when withholding documents within Exemption 7(A)?
questions.question_body: Section IV.C mentions that when an agency withholds documents on a category-by-category basis, it must use categories that are 'sufficiently distinct' to allow a court to determine exemptions. The plaintiff here conceded that the various categories identified by the FBI were overbroad. On what grounds does the D.C. Circuit hold that a plaintiff forfeits these arguments, and is there a procedural timeline requirement for challenging the distinctness of withholding categories during summary judgment?
